\section*{Plale Lab Shared Glossary and Operational Definitions}
Version 0.5 / 2026-10-10
A shared reference for research and engineering: compare meanings, inspect their boundaries, and follow the evidence.

Read in the order Workflow, Harness, Model, LLM, Agent, Schema. The sequence is a reading path, not a claim that all six form a single subtype hierarchy.

External evidence and internal adoption are separate. Each working definition remains a proposal until the lab records consensus.

\subsection*{Source policy}
Research applicable formal institutional definitions first, then peer-reviewed papers, then industry standards, first-party documentation, preprints and academic materials, and finally Lab internal proposals.

Verify the original text, edition, publication status and context. A corporate engineering blog belongs to tier 3. Hosting a paper at a university does not change its publication type.

Prefer relevance over an unrelated authority. Preserve attributed disagreements, record source gaps, and do not turn a single paper into a consensus statement.

Citations accompany definitions, boundaries and typed relations. An editorial inference is marked explicitly; a source citation identifies its basis, not an endorsement of our inference.

\subsection*{Lab adoption}
Yellow means Plale Lab  /  Proposed / not ratified. Green means Plale Lab  /  Adopted by consensus and requires an explicit unanimous decision, date, accessible decision link and evidence record. A merge, publication or authoritative external source does not establish Lab adoption.
\subsection*{Licensing}
Original handbook prose: CC BY 4.0. Build scripts and site code: MIT. Third-party sources retain their own rights.

\newpage\hypertarget{term-workflow}{}
\section*{Workflow}
Process, description, execution
An arrangement of activities and control rules for carrying out a process. Distinguish the process, its description, and the system that executes it. \cite{workflow-patterns,wfmc-1998} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Definition comparison}
\subsubsection*{WfMC terminology}
Institutional; business automation
WfMC describes partial or complete business-process automation, with work or information passed between participants under procedural rules. \cite{wfmc-1998,wfmc-glossary}
\subsubsection*{Workflow Patterns}
Peer-reviewed; control flow
A process definition specifies activities and routing; an instance enacts that definition for a particular case. The paper evaluates static control-flow patterns. \cite{workflow-patterns}
\subsubsection*{LLM engineering}
First-party; narrower architecture
Anthropic calls predefined code paths coordinating LLMs and tools workflows, and contrasts them with model-directed agents. This is an architectural convention within LLM applications. \cite{anthropic-agents}
\subsection*{Scope}
This entry uses Workflow broadly for research and engineering. WfMC places it in business-process automation; its narrower historical definition does not itself define every scientific or Python workflow. \cite{wfmc-1998,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Includes}
\begin{itemize}
\item Editorial example: a deterministic Python load  ->  validate  ->  transform  ->  save pipeline has activities, dependencies and a completion condition. An LLM is unnecessary for our broader working usage. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item Editorial example: a fixed retrieve  ->  summarize  ->  verify LLM pipeline is a workflow even when individual model outputs vary. Fixed control flow does not imply deterministic outputs. \cite{anthropic-agents} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Excludes and counterexamples}
\begin{itemize}
\item A scheduler or execution engine is an implementation that runs work, not the process description itself. \cite{wfmc-1998,workflow-patterns} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item A list of unrelated functions with no stated dependencies or process purpose fails our operational test. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Different usages and open boundaries}
\begin{itemize}
\item Workflow may name a process arrangement, a stored definition, or a run in casual usage. State which object is meant before comparing implementations. \cite{workflow-patterns} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item Predefined paths are not a universal requirement: WfMC distinguishes production workflows from ad-hoc workflows whose procedural rules can change during execution. \cite{wfmc-glossary}
\item The 2003 patterns cover static control flow, not all resource allocation, exceptions or transaction semantics. Do not treat their scope as a universal exclusion rule. \cite{workflow-patterns}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Operational criteria}
Lab test: identify a purpose, activities, dependencies or transition rules, and a completion or termination condition. Label the artifact as description, execution instance or executor. These are editorial criteria, not a quoted standard. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Concept relationships}
Only is-a means a strict subtype. Uses and supports/orchestrates describe composition and control.
Workflow uses LLM\par An LLM workflow uses an LLM for one or more tasks; many workflows use no language model. \cite{anthropic-agents} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Workflow uses Agent\par A designed workflow may delegate an activity to an agent; this is composition, not a claim that every workflow is agentic. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Harness supports/orchestrates Workflow\par A harness realizes or coordinates workflows; runtime-to-process is not strict subtype nesting. \cite{asd-harness,anthropic-harness} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Schema supports/orchestrates Workflow\par Supports a workflow at data-interpretation or validation boundaries; it supplies a description or contract, not the executing control flow. This is a supporting-artifact relation, not a subtype. \cite{xsd-1-1,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Lab working definition}
\textcolor{proposal}{Plale Lab  /  Proposed / not ratified}
No consensus decision recorded.
Use Workflow for an organized process with explicit coordination rules, independent of whether its tasks are manual, deterministic code or model calls. Keep the executor separate from the process it realizes. \cite{lab-guide-v1}

\subsection*{Sources and research gaps}
Institutional scope gap: the historical WfMC definition concerns business automation. The broader Python example and our minimum operational test are explicit Lab proposals.

Retrieval limitation: indexed original excerpts verified the WfMC cover, glossary version and relevant definitions; direct retrieval of the two WfMC PDFs failed.

\cite{wfmc-1998} Tier 1 / Institutional white paper. Context: Business-process automation; quotes the WfMC glossary. Verification: Cover and page 8 verified through indexed excerpts of the original PDF and the official publication catalogue. Direct PDF retrieval failed; no claim of full-document review.
\cite{wfmc-glossary} Tier 1 / Institutional terminology specification. Context: Production and ad-hoc business workflow. Verification: Version and page 8 verified in indexed original excerpts and the official publication catalogue. Direct PDF retrieval failed.
\cite{workflow-patterns} Tier 2 / Peer-reviewed journal article. Context: Business workflow control-flow patterns; not an exhaustive theory of every process. Verification: Final published PDF read; peer-review status, journal and DOI checked against the TU/e publication record.
\cite{anthropic-agents} Tier 3 / First-party engineering blog. Context: Company-specific distinction between predefined LLM workflows and dynamic agents. Verification: Original text and publication record checked 2026-10-10.
\cite{lab-guide-v1} Tier 4 / Lab internal proposal; not ratified. Context: Internal proposals and editorial interpretations, not external consensus. Verification: Version 1.1 adds an explicitly unratified Schema editorial extension; all prior 1.0 sections are retained. No adoption decision claimed.

\newpage\hypertarget{term-harness}{}
\section*{Harness}
The execution layer around a model
In agentic AI, a harness is software around a model that connects it to context and tools and controls execution. Sources differ on whether this means the control loop or the wider non-model runtime. \cite{asd-harness,anthropic-harness} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Definition comparison}
\subsubsection*{ASD advisory}
Institutional; security and governance
ASD uses harness for the non-LLM components of an agentic system, including connections to tools, data, memory and planning workflows, privileges and the control loop. \cite{asd-harness}
\subsubsection*{SWE-agent architecture}
Peer-reviewed; agent-computer interface
SWE-agent supplies a task-oriented interface for a language-model agent to navigate repositories, edit files and execute tests. This informs the runtime boundary; the paper is not treated as a general definition of Harness. \cite{swe-agent} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsubsection*{Managed Agents architecture}
First-party; product boundary
Anthropic separates session, harness and sandbox. Its harness drives the loop and routes model-requested tool calls; the sandbox executes them. \cite{anthropic-harness}
\subsubsection*{Conceptual proposal}
Preprint; not established consensus
Macedo proposes an operational boundary against SDKs, frameworks, IDE plugins, evaluation scaffolds and orchestrators. This is one author's definition proposal. \cite{harness-preprint}
\subsection*{Scope}
Focus here is an agent runtime harness. An evaluation harness instead runs tasks and measures results; a framework or SDK supplies construction abstractions and may include a runtime. Shared naming does not make these identical objects. \cite{harness-preprint} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Includes}
\begin{itemize}
\item Lab example: a running loop that assembles context, dispatches tools, records outcomes and applies stop or permission rules qualifies under our working definition. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item A harness can realize fixed workflows as well as dynamic agent loops. Describe its actual control responsibilities rather than inferring them from a product name. \cite{asd-harness,anthropic-harness} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Excludes and counterexamples}
\begin{itemize}
\item Model weights alone do not supply the surrounding runtime. \cite{asd-harness} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item An SDK import or workflow diagram alone does not demonstrate a running harness. An evaluation runner is labeled evaluation harness unless it also has the claimed agent-runtime responsibilities. \cite{harness-preprint} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Different usages and open boundaries}
\begin{itemize}
\item ASD's broad organizational boundary and Anthropic's separated runtime components answer different questions. Neither establishes that a harness is a kind of process. \cite{asd-harness,anthropic-harness} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item A runtime may be delivered inside an SDK or framework; packaging and execution responsibility are separate axes. \cite{harness-preprint} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Operational criteria}
Lab test: locate the running component responsible for model invocation, context/tool mediation, execution feedback and termination or privilege policy. State where session storage and tool execution live. If the software only constructs that component, label it a framework or SDK. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Concept relationships}
Only is-a means a strict subtype. Uses and supports/orchestrates describe composition and control.
Harness supports/orchestrates Workflow\par A harness realizes or coordinates workflows; runtime-to-process is not strict subtype nesting. \cite{asd-harness,anthropic-harness} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Harness supports/orchestrates Agent\par When it supplies the running loop, tools and execution policy for an agent. \cite{asd-harness} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Harness uses LLM\par In an LLM-based agent runtime; evaluation harnesses and other harness usages have different scopes. \cite{asd-harness,harness-preprint} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Lab working definition}
\textcolor{proposal}{Plale Lab  /  Proposed / not ratified}
No consensus decision recorded.
Use agent harness for the model-surrounding execution layer that mediates context, tools, feedback and control policy. Treat "a specialized workflow" as the initial proposal to discuss, not the adopted subtype taxonomy. \cite{lab-guide-v1}

\subsection*{Sources and research gaps}
Peer-reviewed definition gap: this review did not establish a directly applicable peer-reviewed consensus definition of agent harness. The conceptual paper is a June 2026 preprint, not promoted to tier 2.

\cite{asd-harness} Tier 1 / Institutional security advisory. Context: Organizational security and governance of agentic AI; not a universal taxonomy. Verification: Original text and publication record checked 2026-10-10.
\cite{swe-agent} Tier 2 / Peer-reviewed conference paper. Context: Software-engineering agent architecture; relevant runtime evidence, not a universal harness definition. Verification: Published NeurIPS proceedings PDF and conference record checked 2026-10-10.
\cite{anthropic-harness} Tier 3 / First-party engineering blog. Context: Architecture of a specific hosted agent product. Verification: Original text and publication record checked 2026-10-10.
\cite{harness-preprint} Tier 3 / Preprint; peer review not established. Context: A proposed operational definition in coding-agent engineering; no consensus claim. Verification: Original text and publication record checked 2026-10-10.

\newpage\hypertarget{term-model}{}
\section*{Model}
Representation and inference component
Model has several scopes: a representation of a subject; an executable representation; or, in AI, the inference component transforming inputs into outputs. State the scope before using the term. \cite{nasa-model,eu-us-ai} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Definition comparison}
\subsubsection*{General representation}
Institutional; NASA modeling and simulation
NASA defines a model as a description or representation of a system, entity, phenomenon or process. It separately defines conceptual and computational models. \cite{nasa-model}
\subsubsection*{Computational representation}
Institutional; NASA terminology
A computational model is a usable implementation of a conceptual model, including mathematical, numerical, logical or qualitative representations. Executability alone does not specify what is represented. \cite{nasa-model} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsubsection*{AI inference component}
Institutional; AI-system context
The EU-U.S. terminology identifies a model as a core AI-system component that infers outputs from inputs. This context is narrower than every possible software function. \cite{eu-us-ai} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Scope}
A model need not be learned. NASA's modeling-and-simulation sense includes conceptual representations, while the AI terminology concerns an inference component within a system. \cite{nasa-model,eu-us-ai} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Includes}
\begin{itemize}
\item Editorial examples: a conceptual climate description and its numerical simulation fit representation-oriented usage; a trained classifier fits learned inference usage. These are distinct cases under a broad term. \cite{nasa-model,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item An LLM is one specialized learned model, rather than a synonym for all models. \cite{eu-us-ai} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Excludes and counterexamples}
\begin{itemize}
\item "Any input  ->  output" is insufficient as a universal definition: it omits what the artifact represents and collapses ordinary utilities into model terminology. We retain it only as an internal proposal. \cite{nasa-model,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item An application containing a model, orchestration and tools is a system; the model name should identify its inference component. \cite{eu-us-ai,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Different usages and open boundaries}
\begin{itemize}
\item In learned-model usage, identify the fitted parameters and inference rule; in conceptual-model usage, identify the referent and assumptions. Do not silently require training for all models. \cite{nasa-model,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item A fixed formula may be a model when it represents a stated phenomenon. Being deterministic neither establishes nor prevents that role. \cite{nasa-model} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Operational criteria}
Lab test: record the intended sense, represented subject or inference task, assumptions, inputs and outputs if executable, and whether parameters were learned. For learned models, distinguish the checkpoint from deployment and orchestration. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Concept relationships}
Only is-a means a strict subtype. Uses and supports/orchestrates describe composition and control.
LLM is-a Model\par Within learned AI-model usage: an LLM is a specialized language model, hence a Model. \cite{eu-us-ai} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Agent uses Model\par When a computational model supplies inference or action selection; this is a component relation. \cite{react,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Lab working definition}
\textcolor{proposal}{Plale Lab  /  Proposed / not ratified}
No consensus decision recorded.
Default to a representation or inference component with an explicit subject or task. Use "learned model" when training matters. The broader "any input-to-output mapping" guide remains a pending alternative, not our universal definition. \cite{lab-guide-v1}

\subsection*{Sources and research gaps}
Scope gap: NASA's general representation terminology applies to modeling and simulation; it does not settle every AI use. The EU-U.S. AI meaning and the internal mapping proposal are shown separately.

\cite{nasa-model} Tier 1 / Institutional technical standard. Context: Models and simulations supporting NASA activities. Verification: Final B PDF checked. Portal historical Change Date is inconsistent with its B document date; this record follows the PDF cover, not that legacy field.
\cite{eu-us-ai} Tier 1 / Institutional terminology document. Context: AI-system terminology for transatlantic risk-management and standards cooperation. Verification: Original text and publication record checked 2026-10-10.
\cite{lab-guide-v1} Tier 4 / Lab internal proposal; not ratified. Context: Internal proposals and editorial interpretations, not external consensus. Verification: Version 1.1 adds an explicitly unratified Schema editorial extension; all prior 1.0 sections are retained. No adoption decision claimed.

\subsection*{Related terms}
\hyperlink{term-llm}{LLM}; \hyperlink{term-agent}{Agent}
\newpage\hypertarget{term-llm}{}
\section*{LLM}
Large language model
A large language model is a deep learning language model trained on very large textual datasets. It is a kind of Model; its complete application or agent runtime is a separate system. \cite{eu-us-ai,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Definition comparison}
\subsubsection*{EU-U.S. terminology}
Institutional; language models
The second edition emphasizes deep learning and extremely large text datasets, and includes models that generate text or form representations useful for downstream tasks. \cite{eu-us-ai}
\subsubsection*{GPT-3 study}
Peer-reviewed; a specific experimental scale
Brown and colleagues study an autoregressive model with 175 billion parameters alongside smaller models. Its training corpus mixes web sources, books and Wikipedia; that recipe is an example, not a definition. \cite{gpt3}
\subsection*{Scope}
This page concerns learned language models, including text generation and representation uses. The word "large" needs a stated scale and comparison context. \cite{eu-us-ai,gpt3} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Includes}
\begin{itemize}
\item A trained text-generation checkpoint is a model artifact; adding retrieval, tools and execution control creates a larger application around it. \cite{anthropic-agents,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item Representation-producing language models are within the cited institutional usage; generation is not its only permitted behavior. \cite{eu-us-ai}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Excludes and counterexamples}
\begin{itemize}
\item A corpus alone is training material, not a trained model. A tool-connected assistant is not identical to the language model inside it. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item No universal parameter cutoff is established by the sources used here. Report parameters, training tokens and the relevant comparison rather than inventing a threshold. \cite{gpt3,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Different usages and open boundaries}
\begin{itemize}
\item The institutional definition foregrounds textual training. For a multimodal product, specify its language-model component and additional modalities instead of assuming the same definition covers the whole system. \cite{eu-us-ai,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item Training a model and conditioning an inference call are different operations: the GPT-3 few-shot experiments add examples in context without gradient updates. \cite{gpt3}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Operational criteria}
Lab test: identify the learned model artifact, language task and objective, available training-material evidence, and reported scale. Record unknown proprietary details as unknown. Separately identify any tokenizer, serving system, tools and controller. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Concept relationships}
Only is-a means a strict subtype. Uses and supports/orchestrates describe composition and control.
Workflow uses LLM\par An LLM workflow uses an LLM for one or more tasks; many workflows use no language model. \cite{anthropic-agents} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Harness uses LLM\par In an LLM-based agent runtime; evaluation harnesses and other harness usages have different scopes. \cite{asd-harness,harness-preprint} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
LLM is-a Model\par Within learned AI-model usage: an LLM is a specialized language model, hence a Model. \cite{eu-us-ai} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Agent uses LLM\par For LLM-based agents only; general agents need not use a language model. \cite{react,anthropic-agents} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Lab working definition}
\textcolor{proposal}{Plale Lab  /  Proposed / not ratified}
No consensus decision recorded.
Use LLM for a learned language-model component at a documented large scale. Avoid reducing the term to corpus size alone or using it as the name for a tool-using system. No minimum parameter count is ratified by the lab. \cite{lab-guide-v1}

\subsection*{Sources and research gaps}
Scale gap: the institutional definition supplies qualitative scale, not a universal threshold; a concrete GPT-3 size cannot settle the category for all architectures.

\cite{eu-us-ai} Tier 1 / Institutional terminology document. Context: AI-system terminology for transatlantic risk-management and standards cooperation. Verification: Original text and publication record checked 2026-10-10.

\newpage\hypertarget{term-agent}{}
\section*{Agent}
Goal-directed action with feedback
In general computing, an agent is a situated system with some control over its actions, responsiveness to its environment and goal-directed behavior. LLM-based agents are one implementation, not the whole category. \cite{wooldridge-agent,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Definition comparison}
\subsubsection*{Classical weak agency}
Peer-reviewed; general computing
Wooldridge and Jennings characterize a weak notion through autonomy, social ability, reactivity and pro-activeness. This influential characterization is attributed, not presented as the only universal test. \cite{wooldridge-agent}
\subsubsection*{Institutional project scoping}
NIST draft; identity and authorization
The NCCoE concept paper describes autonomous decisions and actions under limited human supervision toward goals. It is a draft project-scoping document, not a final general-agent standard. \cite{nist-agent-draft}
\subsubsection*{LLM engineering}
First-party; architectural distinction
Anthropic distinguishes predefined workflows from agents whose LLM dynamically directs the process and tool use. Its usage is narrower than general agent theory. \cite{anthropic-agents}
\subsection*{Scope}
Begin with general software or hardware agency. For LLM engineering, explicitly identify the model, action interface and feedback loop; access to a tool alone does not settle agency. \cite{wooldridge-agent,anthropic-agents} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Includes}
\begin{itemize}
\item Editorial example: a goal-directed robot controller can be an agent without an LLM. A software agent can act through commands in a virtual environment. \cite{wooldridge-agent,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item Bounded autonomy can coexist with approval gates. Record which decisions the system controls and which require a person. \cite{nist-agent-draft,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Excludes and counterexamples}
\begin{itemize}
\item A bare text-completion call does not, by itself, show goal-directed interaction with an environment under our test. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item A fixed tool pipeline is not automatically an agent in the dynamic-control engineering sense, even if it contains an LLM and an API. \cite{anthropic-agents} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Different usages and open boundaries}
\begin{itemize}
\item Planning, long-term memory and self-learning are not universal prerequisites in our working definition. Capability claims should be tested separately from the name Agent. \cite{wooldridge-agent,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item We retain autonomy, goal direction, environment feedback and action as Lab criteria. Social ability is explicit in the classical weak notion, but is not a mandatory gate in our narrower operational proposal. \cite{wooldridge-agent,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{LLM-based agents}
An LLM-based agent places a language model within an action-and-observation system. ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions that obtain external information, allowing later reasoning to respond to outcomes. It is one architecture, not a requirement that every agent expose a chain of thought. \cite{react} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

Distinguish choosing an action, granting permission and executing it. A model's proposed tool call does not itself execute a tool; the surrounding runtime provides that capability. \cite{anthropic-harness,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Operational criteria}
Lab test: identify a goal, observations, an action interface, the decisions controlled by the system, and how outcomes affect later actions. For an LLM-based agent, trace a model-selected action, its execution and returned feedback. State stopping and approval conditions. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Concept relationships}
Only is-a means a strict subtype. Uses and supports/orchestrates describe composition and control.
Workflow uses Agent\par A designed workflow may delegate an activity to an agent; this is composition, not a claim that every workflow is agentic. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Harness supports/orchestrates Agent\par When it supplies the running loop, tools and execution policy for an agent. \cite{asd-harness} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Agent uses LLM\par For LLM-based agents only; general agents need not use a language model. \cite{react,anthropic-agents} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
Agent uses Model\par When a computational model supplies inference or action selection; this is a component relation. \cite{react,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Lab working definition}
\textcolor{proposal}{Plale Lab  /  Proposed / not ratified}
No consensus decision recorded.
Use Agent for a system with bounded autonomy, a goal, environment feedback and an ability to act. Use LLM-based agent when an LLM participates in selecting actions. The agent uses a model; it is not classified as an LLM subtype. \cite{lab-guide-v1}

\subsection*{Sources and research gaps}
Institutional definition gap: the NIST material checked is a draft identity/authorization concept paper. No final, general-agent institutional definition was established in this review; the classical peer-reviewed account remains central.

\cite{wooldridge-agent} Tier 2 / Peer-reviewed journal article; author-hosted text. Context: General software/hardware agency, predating LLM engineering. Verification: Author HTML checked; its 1994 conversion timestamp is not the publication year. Journal issue and DOI verified at Cambridge.

\section*{Schema}
Data schema
A schema describes how data is organized and what its fields mean, with structural or value constraints where specified. State the data model and dialect: the exact obligations depend on the schema language. \cite{cnssi-schema,xsd-1-1,json-schema-2020-12} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Definition comparison}
\subsubsection*{Institutional terminology}
CNSSI 4009-2022, reproduced by NIST CSRC; information-security context
CNSSI describes an object through its organization, field syntax, meanings and associated metadata. This is broader than a list of column names. \cite{cnssi-schema}
\subsubsection*{XML validation}
XSD 1.1; W3C Recommendation
XSD separates abstract schema components from their XML schema documents; a validator applies a conforming schema to an XML instance. \cite{xsd-1-1}
\subsubsection*{JSON description}
Draft 2020-12 Core; first-party Internet-Draft
JSON Schema describes an instance using an object or boolean schema. Assertions constrain instances; annotations supply information for applications. \cite{json-schema-2020-12}
\subsubsection*{Data-derived summary}
Goldman and Widom, VLDB 1997; semistructured databases
DataGuides provide structural summaries generated from a database, serving as dynamic schemas for browsing and querying. Their scope is observed structure in that database. \cite{dataguides-1997}
\subsection*{Scope}
Here, schema means a data-description artifact used for interpretation or validation. Psychological schemata and prediction models are outside this entry. \cite{cnssi-schema,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Includes}
\begin{itemize}
\item Named fields, types, permitted structure and explicit constraints; meanings or metadata may also be documented. A schema need not specify every aspect of domain interpretation. \cite{cnssi-schema,json-schema-2020-12} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Excludes and counterexamples}
\begin{itemize}
\item A particular record is a data instance, not the rules applied to it. For example, \{"temperature": 23.5\} supplies a value; a schema separately describes the property and its constraints. \cite{json-schema-2020-12} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item A validator is software that applies a schema. The schema itself is neither that execution nor an entire workflow. \cite{xsd-1-1,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Different usages and open boundaries}
\begin{itemize}
\item Schema may mean declared requirements or a summary inferred from existing data. A DataGuide follows the database; a declared contract can reject data that fails its requirements. Label which direction is intended. \cite{dataguides-1997,xsd-1-1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\item The schema/instance distinction is a role distinction: a JSON schema is itself an instance when checked against a meta-schema. JSON syntax alone does not identify that role. \cite{json-schema-2020-12}
\end{itemize}
\subsection*{Relation to schema extraction}
Schema extraction is the process; a recovered or inferred schema is its output. DataGuides illustrate inference from instances. Recovering an explicitly declared schema is a different evidence task from generalizing observed records. \cite{dataguides-1997,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

For Lab work, retain source-to-field evidence and label observed, declared and inferred constraints. An absent field in a sample does not by itself establish that the field is forbidden; a structural summary alone does not prove complete intended semantics. \cite{dataguides-1997,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Operational criteria}
Identify the described population, schema version/dialect, fields and constraints; distinguish declared rules from observed patterns and unknowns. Show how an example instance is interpreted or checked without treating that example as evidence for every possible record. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Concept relationships}
Only is-a means a strict subtype. Uses and supports/orchestrates describe composition and control.
Schema supports/orchestrates Workflow\par Supports a workflow at data-interpretation or validation boundaries; it supplies a description or contract, not the executing control flow. This is a supporting-artifact relation, not a subtype. \cite{xsd-1-1,lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}
\subsection*{Lab working definition}
\textcolor{proposal}{Plale Lab  /  Proposed / not ratified}
No consensus decision recorded.
Proposed Lab meaning: an explicit, versioned description of data structure, field meanings and stated constraints. Record whether it is declared, recovered from a specification, or inferred from observed data, together with evidence and unresolved coverage. \cite{lab-guide-v1} \textit{Editorial interpretation.}

\subsection*{Sources and research gaps}
The applicable institutional definition was verified through the NIST reproduction; the linked original CNSSI document was not retrievable in this review.

The peer-reviewed DataGuides example supports one semistructured-data approach. This review does not establish a universal definition of schema extraction across paper, database and metadata workflows.

\cite{cnssi-schema} Tier 1 / Institutional terminology; source-attributed glossary reproduction. Context: Object organization, field syntax, semantics and metadata in information-security terminology. Verification: NIST reproduction and its CNSSI attribution checked. The linked CNSS original could not be retrieved; no claim of direct review or a universal NIST-preferred definition.
\cite{dataguides-1997} Tier 2 / Peer-reviewed conference paper. Context: Data-derived structural summaries for the Lore semistructured database; one method, not a universal definition of extraction. Verification: Conference PDF abstract/introduction and proceedings publication record checked. The search engine crawl date is not the publication date.
\cite{xsd-1-1} Tier 3 / W3C Recommendation. Context: Schemas and schema-validity assessment for XML; not a definition of all research metadata. Verification: Dated Recommendation and cited sections checked, rather than an earlier Working Draft.
\cite{json-schema-2020-12} Tier 3 / First-party specification; IETF Internet-Draft, not an RFC. Context: The JSON Schema dialect and instance data model; assertions and annotations have different roles. Verification: Dated Core text and definitions checked. The document identifies itself as an Internet-Draft with intended Informational status; it is not relabeled a final IETF standard.
\cite{lab-guide-v1} Tier 4 / Lab internal proposal; not ratified. Context: Internal proposals and editorial interpretations, not external consensus. Verification: Version 1.1 adds an explicitly unratified Schema editorial extension; all prior 1.0 sections are retained. No adoption decision claimed.

\newpage\hypertarget{lab-guide}{}
\section*{Plale Lab terminology guide}
Version 1.1 / 2026-10-10
\textcolor{proposal}{Plale Lab  /  Proposed / not ratified}
No consensus decision recorded.
\subsection*{Workflow and Harness}
Initial proposal: Workflow is a general arrangement of work; deterministic Python code as well as LLM-based work can participate in a workflow.

Initial proposal: a harness is a workflow designed for an LLM or agent. Editorial revision for discussion: distinguish the execution layer from the process it supports. This edition uses supports/orchestrates rather than declaring a Harness is-a Workflow relationship.

\subsection*{Model and LLM}
Initial proposal: any input-to-output mapping may be called a model. This remains an intentionally broad, unratified interpretation, not a universal external definition.

Working revision: specify whether model means a representation, an executable representation, or a learned inference component. An LLM is a learned language model; its training, scale and scope should be described rather than reduced to an arbitrary parameter threshold.

\subsection*{Agent}
Initial proposal: an agent builds on an LLM and external tools, with its distinguishing attributes still to be decided.

Working revision: reserve the general term for systems with bounded autonomy, goal-directed behavior, environmental feedback and an ability to act. Describe an LLM-based agent as one particular implementation using an LLM. Planning, persistent memory and self-learning are optional capabilities, not automatic universal requirements.

\subsection*{Editorial and adoption policy}
Check external evidence in the fixed order: applicable institutional definitions, peer-reviewed papers, industry standards or first-party documents or preprints or academic materials, then internal proposals. Preserve uncertainty and differing scopes.

Use cited statements, typed relations and a quiet reading layout. Strict nesting is reserved for supported is-a relations. All proposals in this guide are unratified; only a documented consensus decision may authorize green adoption tags.

\subsection*{Schema: an unratified editorial extension}
Proposed extension: use schema for an explicit, versioned description of data structure, field meanings and stated constraints. Keep the data instance, the description and the validator separate; the same document can occupy different roles under a meta-schema.

Schema extraction is a process that recovers declarations or infers a description from evidence. Record the input population, source-to-field evidence, dialect/version, observed versus declared or inferred constraints, and unresolved coverage. A sample is not proof of every permitted record or intended semantic rule.
